chapter: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
title: What the blues really are, and why they are not sinful
summary: Modern singers who spell out their troubles are not blues singers; blues are a story from the soul like Mahalia's spirituals, not sinful.

blocks.x: No. That's the truth. That's the truth. A lot of them. Because I know several of the girls, right now, they would never have made it, and they're big timers now, but they never would have made it in those days, you know. And then, another thing, Chris, a lot of the things that they're calling blues are not blues that they're singing now, and these people, type of blues singers, they're not blues singers.
These people don't know blues, do they? You know, when we were singing the blues, for instance, if I

felt down, you know, maybe troubled, and I had it all my days, I'm telling you about it. These people -- first of all, if they would say what they are trying to say, if they would say it out loud, it's not blues. You know, they don't know blues.
You know, Alberta, you're a religious woman, and you know, I've met quite a few performers.
Who turned to religion in later life.
And very often the religious people look on the blues as sort of a sinful music. You know, Lil's mother, for instance.
But you don't seem to look on the blues as anything sinful.
Well, blues aren't sinful. You're telling a story.

Blues aren't sinful. Blues is a song from your soul. When you're singing the blues, you're singing -- the singers, as Mahalia, who was one of the greatest on earth, was singing a spiritual about some day my time will come, when she's singing that. When I'm singing, "Trouble, trouble, I've had it all my days," I'm feeling that I've had it
so long maybe some day my trouble will pass away.
